purpose: Methazolamide is used to lower the pressure inside your eyes, a condition called glaucoma. High eye pressure can damage your vision over time if left untreated. This medicine helps protect your eyesight by keeping that pressure under control.
how_it_works: Your eyes naturally produce a fluid that can build up and cause pressure. Methazolamide works by blocking a protein in your body called carbonic anhydrase, which slows down how much of that fluid is made. Less fluid means less pressure inside your eye.
common_side_effects: Tingling or numbness in your hands, feet, or face is very common. You may also feel tired, dizzy, or have an upset stomach, nausea, or loss of appetite. Some people notice a metallic taste in their mouth or need to urinate more often.
warnings: Tell your doctor if you are allergic to sulfa drugs, as this medicine is related to that family. It can cause low levels of potassium or sodium in your blood, so let your doctor know if you feel very weak or have muscle cramps. Avoid this medicine if you have severe kidney or liver disease. Drink plenty of fluids to help prevent kidney stones, which are a rare but possible risk. Do not take it if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant without talking to your doctor first.
typical_dosing: The usual dose is 50 to 100 mg taken by mouth two to three times a day. Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on your eye pressure and how well you respond to the medicine. Try to take it at the same times each day and do not stop without asking your doctor first.
